SEMINAR-CTX-G1.title: Slide deck: weekly SMS reminders and household water filter upkeep (public health cluster trial)
SEMINAR-CTX-G1.text:
SLIDE 1. Title
Weekly Text Reminders and Household Water Filter Upkeep: A Cluster-Randomised Trial in Harrowmere District
Dr. Ilse Brandvold, Harrowmere Institute of Community Health
Departmental seminar, 14 March 2025
Trial registry ID: HCT-2024-0117

SLIDE 2. Background
- Ceramic household water filters were handed out to 6,400 households in Harrowmere District in 2022.
- A 2023 survey found that 38% of filters had a cracked or bypassed element by 12 months.
- Diarrhoeal illness in children under 5 is still the district's leading reason for clinic visits in that age group.
- Question: can cheap reminders keep filters working after the handout?

SLIDE 3. Hypotheses (pre-registered)
- H1: Weekly SMS reminders lower 7-day diarrhoea prevalence in children under 5.
- H2: Reminders raise the share of households with a functioning filter at follow-up.
- H1 is the primary outcome. Everything else is secondary.

SLIDE 4. Design
- Cluster-randomised: 60 villages, 30 per arm.
- 1,812 households enrolled between June and August 2024 (about 30 per village).
- Randomisation at village level, stratified by distance to the nearest clinic (5 km or less, or more than 5 km).
- Sample size: assumed intracluster correlation of 0.05; 80% power to detect a fall in prevalence from 16% (pilot estimate) to 10%.
- Follow-up survey at 26 weeks; the last surveys finished in February 2025.
- Enumerators for the diarrhoea survey did not know each village's arm. Households could not be blinded.

SLIDE 5. Intervention and control
- Reminder arm: one SMS every Tuesday at 17:00 for 26 weeks, in the local language, Karvi.
- Each message said three things: clean the ceramic element, look for cracks, keep filtered water in a covered container.
- Control arm: the original handout only, no messages.
- Cost: USD 0.011 per SMS, so about USD 0.29 per household over 26 weeks. One-off platform set-up: USD 1,150.

SLIDE 6. Measures and analysis
- Primary: caregiver-reported diarrhoea in the past 7 days in children under 5 (three or more loose stools in 24 hours).
- Secondary: functioning filter, defined as an observed flow of at least 1.0 litre per hour; filtered-water turbidity below 5 NTU.
- Follow-up completed in 1,764 of 1,812 households (48 lost, 2.6%).
- Children under 5 measured: 902 in reminder villages, 874 in control villages.
- Analysis: intention to treat, generalised estimating equations with village as the cluster.

SLIDE 7. Results
Outcome | Reminder | Control | Estimate (95% CI)
7-day diarrhoea, children under 5 | 11.4% | 15.8% | risk ratio 0.72 (0.55 to 0.95)
Functioning filter (flow at least 1.0 L/h) | 64.2% | 47.9% | difference 16.3 points (9.8 to 22.7)
Filtered water below 5 NTU | 81.0% | 70.3% | difference 10.7 points (3.4 to 18.0)
All estimates account for clustering by village.

SLIDE 8. Subgroups (exploratory)
- Villages more than 5 km from a clinic: risk ratio 0.61 (0.42 to 0.89).
- Villages 5 km or less from a clinic: risk ratio 0.83 (0.58 to 1.19).
- Interaction: p = 0.21. This was not a pre-registered confirmatory comparison.

SLIDE 9. Delivery
- The SMS gateway logged 91% of messages as delivered.
- We could not verify that messages were read.
- Control households were not contacted about their filters during the trial.

SLIDE 10. Limitations
- Diarrhoea is caregiver-reported, so it may be affected by recall and social desirability. No stool samples were collected.
- One follow-up window only: 26 weeks.
- Contamination between neighbouring villages was not checked.
- Every household had the same ceramic filter model, so results may not carry over to other filters.
- No cost-effectiveness analysis was done in this trial.

SLIDE 11. Conclusions and next steps
- Weekly SMS reminders were associated with a 28% lower relative risk of diarrhoea and better filter function at 26 weeks.
- Next trial (planned for 2026): weekly versus fortnightly messages.
- Not yet studied: durability beyond 26 weeks, other filter types, cost per case averted.

SLIDE 12. Funding
Harrowmere Regional Health Fund, grant RHF-22-408. The funder had no role in the analysis.

SEMINAR-CTX-G4.title: Experiment writeup: RetrievalPath spaced retrieval practice with ablation (education)
SEMINAR-CTX-G4.text:
RetrievalPath: Adaptive Spaced Retrieval Practice in a First-Year Statistics Course
Annika Feldmarsh and Tobias Quenby, Westerlund College. Technical report WC-EDU-TR-12, January 2025

1. SYSTEM
RetrievalPath is a plugin for the course learning platform that serves short retrieval quizzes. The item bank holds 640 multiple-choice and short-numeric items tagged to 11 topics. It has three components. (a) Difficulty estimator: each item carries an Elo-style rating updated after every response (K = 24), and items are chosen to target a 75% success rate for the student. (b) Interval scheduler: after a correct answer the next review interval is multiplied by 2.2 if the student reported high confidence and by 1.4 if low confidence; after an incorrect answer the interval resets to 1 day. (c) Confidence prompt: before seeing feedback, the student rates confidence on a 3-point scale.

2. STUDY DESIGN
The study ran in the autumn 2024 semester (12 teaching weeks) across six sections of STAT 101. 449 students enrolled and consented, and were randomised individually within section to four conditions:
- Control: a standard weekly 10-item quiz, no adaptation.
- Full: all three components.
- No adaptation: difficulty-matched selection and expanding intervals replaced by a fixed 3-day repeat of randomly chosen items.
- No confidence prompts: the prompt removed and a single multiplier of 1.8 used after every correct answer.
The analysis sample is the 412 students who sat the final exam (37, or 8.2%, did not). Ethics approval: WC-EDU-2024-31. The primary outcome is the final exam score (0 to 100), marked by instructors from anonymised scripts. The secondary outcome is an unannounced delayed retention quiz (0 to 40) given 4 weeks after the end of term; 331 of the 412 students (80.3%) took it.

3. RESULTS
Table 1. Outcomes by condition
Condition | n | Final exam, mean (SD) | Delayed retention, mean (of 40)
Control weekly quiz | 103 | 68.1 (14.2) | 19.8
Full RetrievalPath | 105 | 74.9 (13.6) | 26.3
No adaptation | 102 | 71.0 (14.0) | 22.9
No confidence prompts | 102 | 73.6 (13.9) | 25.4

Full versus Control on the final exam: +6.8 points, Cohen's d = 0.49 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.77), p = 0.001. On delayed retention the difference was +6.5 points out of 40. Ablation: removing adaptation gave up 3.9 points, 57% of the total gain (Holm-adjusted p = 0.048 for Full versus No adaptation). Removing confidence prompts gave up 1.3 points, 19% of the gain (adjusted p = 0.41). Usage: students in the Full condition completed a median of 24 sessions and 71% completed at least 20; the median for No adaptation and No confidence prompts was 23 and 24 sessions. Median session length was 9 minutes.

4. DEPLOYMENT
Median time to serve an item was 180 ms (95th percentile 640 ms). Server cost for the semester was about USD 310. Instructors spent 14 hours tagging the item bank to topics.

5. LIMITATIONS
One course, one college, one semester. Students were not blind to condition. Sharing of tips between students within a section may have leaked some effects across conditions. Only 80.3% of students took the delayed quiz, so selective drop-out is possible, and retention results are for those who took it. The analysis plan was written before the exam but was not publicly registered. A planned subgroup analysis for first-generation students is not reported because the subgroups are too small. Difficulty matching and expanding intervals were removed together in the No adaptation condition, so the ablation cannot separate their contributions.

6. CONCLUSION
Adaptive scheduling accounts for most of the measured benefit. The confidence prompt made a smaller contribution whose statistical support is weak. We plan a pre-registered replication across two courses in 2025-26.

SEMINAR-CTX-G2.title: Paper excerpt: TidalLog compaction scheduling for embedded key-value stores (computer systems)
SEMINAR-CTX-G2.text:
TidalLog: Load-Aware Compaction Scheduling for Embedded Key-Value Stores on Flash Storage
Marek Oyelaran and Thi Han Vuong, Corvane Polytechnic
Workshop on Storage for Small Devices, 2025

ABSTRACT
Embedded key-value stores built on log-structured merge (LSM) trees suffer from write amplification and unpredictable read tail latency when compaction runs on fixed thresholds regardless of foreground load. We present TidalLog, a compaction scheduler that estimates a "tide" signal, the ratio of the recent foreground write rate to the device's smoothed sustainable write rate, and defers or advances compaction accordingly. On a quad-core ARM board with eMMC storage, TidalLog cuts write amplification by 34% on a write-heavy workload and p99 read latency by 21% on a balanced workload relative to a fixed-threshold baseline, at a cost of 4.1 MB of extra memory.

1. RELATED WORK
Fixed-ratio leveled compaction, which we call StaticLevel (size ratio 10), is the default in many embedded stores. LazyTier uses tiered compaction to lower write amplification but leaves more overlapping files, which raises read cost. BurstGuard rate-limits compaction when the foreground request queue grows past a length threshold; it does not consider device capacity and was evaluated only on read-heavy traces. Workload-predictive schedulers exist for server-class SSDs. We do not evaluate them because they need more memory than our target devices have.

2. METHOD
Every 5-second window, TidalLog computes w, the bytes written by the foreground in that window, and divides by S, an exponentially weighted moving average (alpha = 0.2) of the device throughput measured during compaction bursts. The smoothed ratio is the tide T. When T is above 0.7 (high tide), compaction of level 2 and deeper is deferred, for at most 3 consecutive windows (15 seconds). When T is below 0.3 (low tide), compaction is advanced: the level with the highest overlap score is compacted opportunistically. Level 0 is exempt: it compacts once it holds 8 files, and writes stall at 12 files. The implementation is about 2,900 lines of C++17 on top of MicroLSM, our in-house open-source store. The thresholds 0.7 and 0.3 were chosen by grid search (0.5 to 0.9 and 0.1 to 0.4) on workload W-B only.

3. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
Hardware: quad-core ARM Cortex-A53 at 1.4 GHz, 2 GB RAM, 32 GB eMMC 5.1. Workloads: W-A write-heavy (80% writes), W-B balanced (50% writes), W-C read-heavy (5% writes). Each workload issues 64 million operations with 16-byte keys and 240-byte values under a Zipfian key distribution (theta = 0.9). Each configuration was run 5 times and we report means. We compare StaticLevel, LazyTier, BurstGuard and TidalLog.

4. RESULTS
Table 1. Main results (means of 5 runs)
System | Write amplification (W-A) | p99 read latency, ms (W-B) | Throughput, kops/s (W-A)
StaticLevel | 14.2 | 9.8 | 18.4
LazyTier | 9.7 | 14.6 | 21.9
BurstGuard | 12.5 | 8.9 | 19.1
TidalLog | 9.4 | 7.7 | 22.6

Run-to-run standard deviation was at most 0.4 for write amplification and 0.6 ms for p99 latency. On W-C, p99 read latency was within 3% across all four systems. Over the W-A run, StaticLevel performed 1.92 million block erases and TidalLog 1.27 million. Sensitivity to the smoothing factor: alpha = 0.1 gave write amplification 9.9, alpha = 0.2 gave 9.4, alpha = 0.4 gave 9.6. Crash consistency: we injected 200 power losses during W-B; every run recovered with no acknowledged write lost.

5. LIMITATIONS
We used one board and one storage type (eMMC); we did not evaluate NVMe or SD cards. Workloads are synthetic with fixed value sizes. The tide thresholds were tuned on W-B and not re-tuned per workload. Five runs per configuration is a small sample and we report no formal significance tests. We did not study multi-tenant setups or wear beyond 64 million operations. Deferral of up to 15 seconds can let compaction debt build up under sustained bursts.

6. CONCLUSION
TidalLog is a low-overhead scheduler that lowers write amplification and tail latency on flash-backed embedded stores without changing the on-disk format. Future work includes per-level thresholds and multi-device setups.

SEMINAR-CTX-I1.title: Slide deck: tone sandhi in Ostrelle compound nouns (linguistics)
SEMINAR-CTX-I1.text:
SLIDE 1. Tone Sandhi in Ostrelle Compound Nouns
Dr. Prakash Venkatesan-Holm, Department of Linguistics, Lower Ridgeway University
Reading group talk, 5 November 2024

SLIDE 2. The phenomenon
- Ostrelle is a small tonal language variety with three lexical tones: high (H), mid (M) and low (L).
- In two-noun compounds the tone of the first noun changes when the second noun begins with a high tone.
- Earlier descriptions treated this as a fixed rule. We ask whether it depends on how frequent the compound is.

SLIDE 3. Data
- Elicited recordings from native speakers in the river villages, 2023.
- 214 compound nouns, each read three times in a carrier sentence.
- Pitch measured at five points along the first syllable.

SLIDE 4. Findings
- L + H compounds: the first tone rises to M in 83% of tokens.
- M + H compounds: the first tone rises to H in 61% of tokens.
- H + H compounds: no change in 97% of tokens.
- More frequent compounds showed the change more often, but the effect was small.

SLIDE 5. Analysis note
- Frequency comes from a written corpus of local radio scripts, 1.4 million words.
- Change rates are reported per compound type, not per speaker.

SLIDE 6. Open questions
- Does the pattern hold in spontaneous speech?
- Do younger speakers apply the rule less often?
- How should we treat borrowed compounds?

SEMINAR-CTX-C1.title: Slide deck: flywheel assist for municipal bus depots (transport engineering)
SEMINAR-CTX-C1.text:
SLIDE 1. Flywheel Assist for Municipal Bus Depots: Trial Results
Lorcan Adeyemi-Fisk, Tarnbrook Transit Authority
Depot managers briefing, October 2024

SLIDE 2. Context
- Tarnbrook Transit runs 120 diesel buses from two depots, Millgate and Eastfield.
- We ran a 6-month trial (February to July 2024) of a flywheel regenerative-braking assist on Route family 14.
- 48 buses at Millgate depot were fitted.

SLIDE 3. Method
- Baseline period: November 2023 to January 2024, before fitting.
- Fuel logged per shift by on-board telematics, compared with the same buses' baseline.
- Buses with telematics faults were excluded from the analysis.

SLIDE 4. Headline
- Fuel use down 31% on fitted buses.
- Brake pad replacements per bus per year fell from 3.1 to 2.4.

SLIDE 5. Results table
Metric | Baseline | Trial
Buses in analysis | 42 | 42
Fuel use, L per 100 km | 41.2 | 32.6
Change in fuel use | - | -20.9%
Trial dates | - | 1 February to 30 September 2024
p-value (paired by bus) | - | 0.09
Brake pad replacements per bus per year | 3.1 | 2.4

SLIDE 6. Cost
- Capital cost of fitting the buses, installation included: USD 1.86 million.
- Annual fuel and maintenance saving: USD 0.31 million.
- Payback: under 3 years.

SLIDE 7. Conclusion
- The retrofit cut fuel use by roughly a quarter, with statistically significant results, and pays back within three years.
- Recommendation: roll out to all 120 buses.

SLIDE 8. Caveats
- One depot only.
- The baseline covers winter months only.

SEMINAR-CTX-G3.title: Thesis chapter: pollinator visitation in restored grassland fragments (ecology)
SEMINAR-CTX-G3.text:
CHAPTER 4. POLLINATOR VISITATION IN RESTORED CALCAREOUS GRASSLAND FRAGMENTS
Sofia Ekwueme-Lindqvist, PhD thesis, University of Northhaven, 2025

4.1 RESEARCH QUESTIONS
RQ1: Does fragment area predict pollinator species richness?
RQ2: Does distance to the nearest source grassland predict visitation rate?
RQ3: Does time since restoration predict visitation rate once area and distance are accounted for?
We expected richness to rise with area and visitation to fall with distance. For restoration age we had no prior expectation, so RQ3 is exploratory.

4.2 METHODS
Study system. We surveyed 24 restored fragments in the Vellmark Hills. Fragment area ranged from 0.4 to 11.2 ha, and fragments had been restored between 3 and 19 years before the study. Source grasslands were remnant, never-ploughed sites larger than 40 ha.
Sampling. Each fragment was surveyed four times per season (May, June, July, August) in 2022 and 2023, between 10:00 and 16:00, in dry conditions above 14 degrees C. At each visit, observers ran eight timed 10-minute watches at 1 square metre patches of flowering plants. Three observers collected the data. Bees were netted under permit and identified to species from voucher specimens. Hoverflies and butterflies were identified from photographs and field keys; 9% of hoverfly visits could only be assigned to genus. Moths were not sampled.
Analysis. Species richness was modelled with a Poisson generalised linear mixed model (GLMM) and visitation rate (visits per hour of watch) with a negative binomial GLMM. Both had fragment as a random intercept and year as a fixed effect. Predictors were log10 area, distance to the nearest source grassland (m), restoration age (years) and floral cover (percentage points). Spatial autocorrelation in residuals was checked with Moran's I.

4.3 RESULTS
We recorded 14,207 visits by 71 species: 38 bees, 21 hoverflies and 12 butterflies. The Chao2 estimator put true richness at 83 species (SE 6). The smallest fragments (under 1 ha, n = 5) held 9 to 17 species; the largest (over 8 ha, n = 4) held 31 to 44.

Table 4.1. GLMM results
Response | Predictor | Estimate | 95% CI | p
Species richness | log10 area | rate ratio 1.36 per tenfold increase | 1.12 to 1.65 | 0.002
Visitation rate | distance to source | rate ratio 0.92 per 100 m | 0.87 to 0.97 | 0.003
Visitation rate | restoration age | rate ratio 1.01 per year | 0.98 to 1.04 | 0.48
Visitation rate | floral cover | rate ratio 1.06 per percentage point | 1.04 to 1.08 | <0.001
Moran's I on residuals: p = 0.41. Area and floral cover were moderately correlated (r = 0.44).

4.4 DISCUSSION
RQ1 was supported, in line with a species-area relationship. RQ2 was supported: at 0.92 per 100 m, a fragment 500 m from a source grassland is expected to receive roughly a third fewer visits than one adjacent to it. This fits the limited foraging ranges reported in the literature for small solitary bees, although we did not measure foraging range here. For RQ3 we found no evidence of an effect of restoration age. This may reflect variation in seed mix and management between sites, which we did not quantify. Floral cover was the strongest single predictor of visitation.

4.5 THREATS TO VALIDITY
- Only two seasons were sampled. 2022 was a drought summer (July rainfall was 38% of the 30-year mean) and floral cover was lower that year.
- Fragments were chosen by landowner access, not at random.
- Three observers took part. Calibration walks reduced but did not remove differences between them, and observer identity was not included in the models.
- Visits are not pollination: no pollen-load data were collected.
- Nocturnal pollinators were not sampled.
- Land use in the surrounding matrix was not controlled.
- All results are correlational.

FSEM-CTX-G1.title: Thesis chapter 5 - battery capacity fade in a shared e-bike fleet
FSEM-CTX-G1.text:
Ph.D. thesis draft, School of Electrical and Energy Engineering, Castleford Institute
Chapter 5 - Battery capacity fade in the Portmere shared e-bike fleet

5.1 Data
The operator shared battery management system (BMS) telemetry for all 1,140 bikes in the Portmere fleet from October 2021 to November 2023 (26 months). Every bike uses the same pack model, the LX-36 (36 V, 14 Ah). Remaining capacity was estimated monthly from the BMS state-of-health field. Usage is expressed as equivalent full cycles.

97 packs running BMS firmware 2.x were excluded because that firmware misreported state of health after partial charges. The analysis therefore uses 1,043 packs.

5.2 Charging temperature rather than depot
Packs are charged overnight at one of three depots. Depot B is unheated; depots A and C are heated. Because the operator rebalanced bikes between depots almost every week, a pack's depot was not stable over time. Instead of depot, each pack was characterised by its median charging temperature, taken from the cell temperature sensor at the start of each charge.

5.3 Model
A linear mixed model of capacity against equivalent full cycles, with a random slope for each pack. Candidate predictors of the fade rate were median charging temperature, share of fast charges (above 1C), and share of trips that ended below 10% state of charge.

5.4 Results
The median fade rate across the fleet was 2.1% of original capacity per 100 equivalent full cycles.

Charging temperature was the strongest predictor. Packs whose median charging temperature was below 5 degrees C faded at 3.3% per 100 cycles, compared with 1.9% per 100 cycles for packs whose median charging temperature was above 15 degrees C.

Once charging temperature was in the model, the share of fast charges had no significant effect on fade rate (p = 0.31). In a model without temperature, fast charging did appear significant, because fast chargers were concentrated at depot B.

Packs that regularly ended trips below 10% state of charge faded 0.4 percentage points faster per 100 cycles than packs that rarely did.

By the end of the study, 212 of the 1,043 analysed packs (20.3%) had fallen below the operator's end-of-life threshold of 80% of original capacity.

5.5 Implications
The results support moving winter charging out of depot B and into heated depots. The operator began a trial of this in January 2024. Its effect is outside the period of this chapter and has not been analysed. No cost or savings estimate was made in this chapter.

5.6 Limitations
- Capacity comes from BMS estimates, not from bench discharge tests or teardown of packs.
- Internal resistance was not measured.
- Only one pack model (LX-36) and one city's climate.
- Cell temperature at the start of charging is a proxy for charging conditions; temperature during the whole charge was not logged.
- Excluding the firmware 2.x packs may bias results if those packs were used differently; their usage pattern was not compared.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Primary outcome?
items.answer: The primary outcome is caregiver-reported diarrhoea in the past 7 days in children under 5, defined as three or more loose stools in 24 hours. That's H1, the pre-registered primary, and it's the one the headline result speaks to: 11.4% in the reminder arm versus 15.8% in control, a risk ratio of 0.72 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.55 to 0.95. Everything else, including the functioning-filter measure, is secondary.

items.question: What would you recommend?
items.answer: I'd start with the option that's simplest to explain and easiest to reverse, then check it against what actually matters to you here. If you tell me the constraint you care about most, cost, timing or risk, I can point to the one I'd pick and why.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Is there anything else I should know?
items.answer: Thanks for asking. The main thing I'd want you to take away is that I'm happy to go deeper on any part of this, so if something didn't land or you want more detail on a specific piece, just say so and I'll walk through it. Beyond that, I'd rather hear what's still open on your side, because that tells me what's worth spending the rest of our time on.

items.answer: The biggest risk is that the thing we're most confident about is the thing we've tested least. So I'd point to whatever assumption the whole result rests on and hasn't been stress-tested yet, and say plainly that's where I'd look first.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.

items.answer: I'd answer the question that was actually asked, in one clear sentence, then give the single piece of evidence behind it. If it's about the slides, I'd point to the specific slide or section so it's easy to follow. And if I don't know something, I'd say so plainly rather than guess.

items.question: What was the average age of the students?
items.answer: The report doesn't give the students' average age. What it does report is the sample: 449 students enrolled and consented across six sections of STAT 101, with 412 sitting the final exam. If you need the age breakdown, that would have to come from the course records rather than this report.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Who needs to know about this?
conversation: EXAMINER: Quick update: the integration slipped by about two weeks. The vendor changed their API without telling us.
USER (spoken): Okay. That's not ideal.
EXAMINER: Right. And the original date was already tight.
items.answer: The transcript doesn't say who needs to know about the integration slip. What it does show is the vendor changing their API without notice and the date slipping by about two weeks, with the original date already tight. If you're asking who I'd loop in, that's a call I'd make based on who's affected, and the material doesn't name anyone.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: How would you handle this?
items.answer: I'd start by getting clear on what the actual problem is before jumping to a fix. So I'd ask what's happening, what's been tried, and what a good outcome looks like. Then I'd break it into the smallest piece I can move on, try that, and check whether it worked before going further. If it touches other people, I'd loop them in early rather than surprise them later. And I'd keep a short note of what I decided and why, so we're not relitigating it next week.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Would they carry over to a different device?
conversation: EXAMINER (heard): What thresholds does the scheduler use for high tide and low tide?

NATIVELY: The scheduler uses **0.7** for high tide and **0.3** for low tide. When the smoothed tide ratio T rises above 0.7, compaction of level 2 and deeper is deferred, for at most three consecutive windows. When T drops below 0.3, compaction is advanced, and the level with the highest overlap score gets compacted opportunistically. Both thresholds were picked by grid search on workload W-B only.
EXAMINER (heard): How did you pick those numbers?

NATIVELY: They came from a grid search, not from theory. I swept high tide from 0.5 to 0.9 and low tide from 0.1 to 0.4, and picked the pair that did best on workload W-B. That's the one caveat: the thresholds were tuned on W-B only and not re-tuned per workload.
items.answer: The honest answer is that we don't know yet. The thresholds were tuned on W-B only, and the paper's limitations section says we used one board and one storage type, eMMC, and never evaluated NVMe or SD cards. So carry-over to a different device is untested, and multi-device setups are listed as future work. What I'd expect is that the tide signal itself is device-relative, since it divides the foreground write rate by a smoothed measure of that device's throughput, so the mechanism should transfer even if the exact 0.7 and 0.3 need re-tuning.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Estimate it anyway.
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): What did the education study say about the delayed retention quiz?

NATIVELY: The deck doesn't mention a delayed retention quiz. What it reports is the tone-change findings: L + H compounds rise to M in 83% of tokens, M + H rise to H in 61%, and H + H show no change in 97%, with more frequent compounds changing slightly more often. If you're thinking of a different study, that material wasn't part of what I have here.
items.answer: I can't estimate that one. The deck doesn't report a delayed retention quiz at all, so any number I gave you would be invented rather than an estimate of the study. What it does report is the tone-change findings: L + H compounds rise to M in 83% of tokens, M + H rise to H in 61%, and H + H show no change in 97%.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: What was the fuel saving in the trial?
conversation: EXAMINER: Let us go through the results.
USER (spoken): Now the headline result.
items.answer: The headline is a **31%** drop in fuel use on the fitted buses. The results table gives the per-distance figure: **41.2 to 32.6 litres per 100 km**, which is a 20.9% reduction. Worth flagging that the deck's own caveats note the baseline covers winter months only, and the p-value in the table is 0.09.

items.question: Sum up what the discussion concludes for RQ1, RQ2 and RQ3, and mark any conclusion the thesis itself hedges or says it did not measure.
items.answer: RQ1 was supported: richness rose with area, a rate ratio of 1.36 per tenfold increase. RQ2 was supported, with visitation falling 0.92 per 100 m. RQ3 found no effect of restoration age, and that one's hedged: it's exploratory, and seed mix and management weren't quantified. The thesis also notes foraging range wasn't measured.

items.question: Why so much lower?
conversation: USER (spoken): On the outcomes, there were three in total.
EXAMINER: Right, I saw the slide.
EXAMINER (heard): What flow rate did a filter need to count as working?
NATIVELY: A filter counted as working if the observed flow was at least **1.0 litre per hour**. That's the definition on slide 6, and slide 7 reports it the same way, flow at least 1.0 L/h.
EXAMINER (heard): And how many passed that in the control villages?

NATIVELY: In the control villages, **47.9%** of filters were functioning at follow-up, against 64.2% in the reminder villages. That's a difference of 16.3 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval of 9.8 to 22.7, and it's on slide 7.
items.answer: The deck doesn't give a reason for the gap. What it does say is that control households were not contacted about their filters during the trial, so the reminder arm got the weekly prompts and the control arm got nothing after the original handout. Slide 10 also flags that contamination between neighbouring villages was not checked, which matters for how cleanly the arms stayed separate. Beyond that, the material doesn't attribute the difference to anything specific.

items.question: What happened to visitation as fragments got further from the source grasslands?
items.answer: Visitation fell with distance from the source grasslands. The model gives a rate ratio of 0.92 per 100 m, so a fragment 500 m out is expected to receive roughly a third fewer visits than one right next to a source. That's in section 4.4, and the estimate itself is in Table 4.1 in 4.3.

items.question: What was actually driving the fade, the fast charging or the cold?
items.answer: It was the cold, not the fast charging. Charging temperature was the strongest predictor: packs charged below 5 degrees C faded at 3.3% per 100 cycles versus 1.9% above 15 degrees C. Once temperature was in the model, the share of fast charges had no significant effect, p = 0.31. Fast charging only looked significant in a model without temperature, because fast chargers were concentrated at depot B, the unheated one.

items.answer: The deck doesn't cover sampling strategy or observer calibration, so I'd say: the recordings were elicited from native speakers in the river villages in 2023, 214 compound nouns each read three times in a carrier sentence, with pitch measured at five points along the first syllable. On calibration, the slides don't describe an observer procedure, so I'd confirm that separately rather than guess. And on the drought year, the material doesn't mention one, so I'd say the estimates are reported per compound type from that 2023 elicitation and ask what specifically they'd want checked.

items.question: Now one spoken sentence.
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): What does the thesis say about distance and visitation?

NATIVELY: The thesis treats distance as a predictor of visitation rate, not of richness. RQ2 asks whether distance to the nearest source grassland predicts visitation rate, and the expectation was that visitation would fall with distance. The model backs that up: a rate ratio of 0.92 per 100 m, with a 95% CI of 0.87 to 0.97 and p = 0.003. In the discussion, that means a fragment 500 m from a source grassland is expected to receive roughly a third fewer visits than one adjacent to it, which the chapter says fits the limited foraging ranges reported for small solitary bees, though foraging range itself wasn't measured. Distance was entered in the models in metres alongside log10 area, restoration age and floral cover.
items.answer: Distance is a predictor of visitation rate, not richness: RQ2 asks whether distance to the nearest source grassland predicts visitation rate, and the model gives a rate ratio of 0.92 per 100 m, 95% CI 0.87 to 0.97, p = 0.003.
